title: Oil Crosses $100 a Barrel Again as the Iran Ceasefire Unravels — This Time the Threat Is to Shipping Lanes, Not Just Supply
summary: Brent crude pushed back above $100 a barrel this week as the fragile truce ending February's US-Israel-Iran war showed fresh signs of collapse, with Iranian strikes on commercial vessels and Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping threatening key transit chokepoints. The move matters less for the price level itself than for what it signals: a conflict many investors had assumed was winding down is instead proving chronic, and energy markets are once again a direct channel into the Fed's inflation calculus.
context:
- The current spike traces back to Operation Epic Fury, the joint US-Israeli strikes launched on 28 February 2026 that killed Iran's supreme leader; a Pakistan-mediated ceasefire followed in April, and a June memorandum of understanding was meant to formalise an end to the conflict within 60 days — but fighting resumed in July after Iran struck three commercial vessels that had bypassed its approved shipping route.

- Unlike earlier supply-shock scares, this round of risk premium is driven mainly by threats to transit routes rather than to production itself: Houthi attacks on shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb strait matter because roughly 12-15% of global maritime trade, worth over $1 trillion a year, passes through that corridor alongside the Strait of Hormuz.

- The ceasefire-violation-resumption cycle has now repeated several times since April, which is why markets are increasingly pricing this as a recurring structural risk rather than a one-off shock — a key reason oil's roughly 35% rise this month has proven sticky rather than fading within days.

- Higher oil directly reshapes the US rates debate: odds of a Fed rate hike later in 2026 reportedly jumped from around 12% to 38% in the space of a week as crude climbed past $100, reinforcing the hawkish tilt Fed officials had already flagged and complicating any case for the rate cuts markets had been pricing earlier in the year.

- With WTI near $92 and Brent above $100, the read-through is that energy costs and monetary policy are now tightly coupled again, leaving the Fed's 28-29 July meeting to weigh a geopolitical, largely un-forecastable variable alongside the domestic inflation data it usually leans on.

title: Burnham Becomes Britain's Fifth PM in Four Years — and Gilt Markets Immediately Remind Him Who Sets the Terms
summary: Andy Burnham took over as UK prime minister this week after Keir Starmer's resignation, appointing John Healey as chancellor, only for gilt yields to jump and sterling to wobble the moment Burnham talked publicly about 'fiscal flexibility'. The episode matters because it shows how little room any new UK leader now has to manoeuvre: bond investors, still scarred by 2022, have become the effective arbiters of British fiscal policy.
context:
- Burnham is Britain's fifth prime minister in just four years, a level of political churn that has left investors trading fiscal signals and personnel changes far more than any policy platform, since none has stayed in place long enough to be judged on delivery.

- The market's hair-trigger sensitivity dates back to Liz Truss's September 2022 mini-budget, when £45 billion of unfunded tax cuts announced without independent forecasts sent 30-year gilt yields from roughly 3.4% to nearly 5% in days and forced an emergency Bank of England intervention; that episode created a standing 'bond vigilante' reflex that has shaped every subsequent UK fiscal announcement.

- Sterling initially rallied to its strongest level since January on reports that the fiscally cautious Shabana Mahmood might become chancellor, then gave back those gains once Burnham himself raised the idea of flexibility within the fiscal rules — underlining that markets are pricing the chancellor and the rules, not the prime minister's own instincts.

- The 10-year gilt yield rose to around 5.04% and the 30-year to about 5.75%, both among the highest in the G7, meaning the UK is already paying a structural borrowing-cost premium versus peers before any actual policy has changed — a reputational risk premium as much as a fiscal one.

- Strategists caution this week's moves are only a preview: the more significant test comes with the full cabinet announcement and the autumn Budget, when Burnham's government will have to show whether 'flexibility' translates into concrete tax and spending decisions.

title: Alphabet and Tesla's Earnings Reopen the AI Capex Debate — Now It's About Depreciation, Not Just Demand
summary: Alphabet and Tesla shares fell sharply this week not because of weak growth but because both raised or blew through capital spending expectations — Alphabet lifted its 2026 capex outlook towards $205 billion even as cloud revenue beat forecasts, while Tesla posted its first negative free cash flow quarter in over two years. The reaction marks a shift in what investors are worried about: not whether AI demand exists, but whether the accounting behind hyperscalers' spending is flattering earnings that free cash flow says are far weaker.
context:
- This follows directly from the semiconductor sell-off earlier in July, which was driven by doubts over AI compute demand; this week's mega-cap declines show the same underlying anxiety migrating up the supply chain to the hyperscalers actually buying that compute, rather than resolving it.

- The scale of the mismatch is the core issue: the largest hyperscalers spent roughly $412 billion on AI capex in 2025 and are on pace for around $760 billion in 2026, yet are only booking about $211 billion in depreciation and amortisation against that spending — leaving hundreds of billions of dollars in outlays not yet reflected in reported costs.

- Critics, including prominent short-sellers, argue hyperscalers are depreciating AI hardware over five to six years when its practical economic life may be closer to two to three given the pace of chip obsolescence — meaning today's reported earnings could be significantly overstating the true, ongoing cost of the AI buildout.

- The headline numbers obscured softer underlying signals: Alphabet's reported profit growth was boosted substantially by paper gains on its stakes in other AI companies rather than core operating performance, while Tesla's negative free cash flow was driven by a sharp jump in capital spending tied to AI, robotics and autonomous systems rather than any weakening in its core car business.

- With Meta, Amazon and Microsoft still to report, this week's reaction sets a more sceptical bar for the rest of Big Tech's AI spending plans, particularly with chip-sector demand concerns still fresh and a Fed now leaning hawkish, leaving growth stocks less room to be forgiven for weak cash generation.
